name: RET rearrangement
summary: RET fusions occur in a small subset of NSCLC, predominantly adenocarcinomas in never-smokers, and are highly sensitive to selective RET inhibitors.
biology: RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase normally involved in neural crest development. Fusions with partners such as KIF5B and CCDC6 juxtapose the RET kinase domain with dimerisation domains, causing constitutive ligand-independent activation of MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways. Older multikinase inhibitors with RET activity were limited by off-target VEGFR toxicity, prompting development of selective agents.
alterations: Acquired RET fusions as resistance to EGFR TKIs
Acquired solvent-front (G810X) and other kinase-domain mutations after selective RET inhibitors

testing.specimen: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumour tissue (biopsy, resection or cytology cell block); plasma ctDNA as a complementary or initial approach
testing.notes: RET IHC is not reliable for fusion detection. FISH may not identify the partner and can miss some rearrangements.

predictiveRelevance: RET fusions predict benefit from selpercatinib and pralsetinib; selective RET inhibition is preferred over chemo-immunotherapy where available. Response to single-agent immunotherapy is generally limited.
resistance: On-target RET solvent-front mutations (G810R/S/C) and hinge-region mutations
Bypass: MET amplification, KRAS amplification or mutation
cnsConsiderations: Brain metastases are common; selpercatinib and pralsetinib have demonstrated intracranial activity.
